newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan polling gets off to slow start.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan polling gets off to slow start.

text.p: Pakistanis began voting on Monday in an election forced by President Farooq Leghari's dismissal of former prime minister Benazir Bhutto three months ago on disputed charges of corruption and misrule.
Very few voters had shown up when polling stations opened across the country at 7:00 a.m. (0200 GMT), an hour earlier than usual due to the Moslem fasting month of Ramadan.

One young voter, Mohammad Agha, waved a key-ring in the shape of a tiger, electoral symbol of Nawaz Sharif's Pakistan Muslim League (PML). "That's who I'm going to vote for and so is everyone else," he said at an Islamabad polling station.
Polling stations were virtually deserted at the start of voting in Islamabad, Karachi, Lahore and elsewhere. The weather was fine in most parts of the country, but foggy in Lahore.

"Unlike the past, there is little public enthusiasm today. I remember there used to be long queues of voters even an hour before the polling started. But today there are hardly any," said Mehjabeen Ghazanfar, an assistant presiding officer at a polling station in Karachi's District East.

Troops guarded the polling stations, while paramilitary rangers patrolled the streets of the volatile port city, where two supporters of the breakaway Mohajir National Movement (MQM) -Haqiqi faction were wounded by gunfire in Moosa Colony of District Central overnight.
The 36,415 polling stations, tightly guarded by police and 250,000 troops on election duty, will stay open until 4:00 p.m. (1100 GMT), with results expected late in the evening.
The main fight pits the PML, fielding 177 National Assembly candidates, against Bhutto's Pakistan People's Party, with 161.

Ex-cricketer Imran Khan's Tehrik-i-Insaaf (Justice Movement) has put up 132 candidates, a splinter PPP group led by Bhutto's bereaved sister-in-law Ghinwa Bhutto 66 and the MQM 55. Others are from smaller parties or are standing as independents.
Leghari promised in an address to the nation on Sunday night that the polls would be free, fair and open.
"By tomorrow night, we will...complete the process of free, fair and transparent elections," he declared on television.
Former prime minister Sharif said he was confident of winning. His main rival, Bhutto, fighting for political survival, has accused the president of planning to rig the vote.
Bhutto rejected any notion she might agree to leave Pakistan to escape possible prosecution for corruption.
"The question does not arise of my seeking asylum in Britain or anywhere else," she told Reuters at her farmhouse in Naudero, near her home town of Larkana, before leaving to cast her vote.
"Pakistan is my home and I am going to live in my home," said Bhutto, who denies any wrongdoing.
The Supreme Court ruled last week that there was enough evidence to justify Leghari's action in sacking Bhutto and threw out the 43-year-old politician's plea for reinstatement.

"My father also lived here. He could have gone abroad. He chose to die here," said a defiant Bhutto, recalling the fate of her father, former prime minister Zulfikar Ali Bhutto, who was toppled by the military in 1977 and executed two years later.

She was responding to a report in London's Sunday Times, which quoted senior Pakistani government sources as saying that to avoid a sensitive trial, possible corruption charges against Bhutto and her jailed husband Asif Ali Zardari could be dropped if she agreed to leave the country and abandon politics.
Zardari has been under detention since Bhutto's government was removed on November 5 and faces a charge of conspiring in the September 20 murder of Benazir's estranged brother Murtaza.
